claim: The percentage of myeloid cells in peripheral blood began to change as early as 6 months in mice and continued to increase at a constant rate until the age of ≥23 months.
source: These results showed that the percentage of myeloid cells began to change as early as 6 months in mice and continued to increase at a constant rate until the age of ≥23 months (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1A showing age-associated changes in peripheral blood cell frequencies across multiple time points.

claim: The frequency of immunophenotypically defined HSC in bone marrow rapidly increased up to the age of 12 months, after which the rate of increase appeared to slow down.
source: We found that the frequency of immunophenotypically defined HSC in BM rapidly increased up to the age of 12 months. After the age, the rate of increase in their frequency appeared to slow down (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow analysis data shown in Figure 1B tracking HSC frequency across different ages.

claim: The frequency of GMP was stable with age.
source: On the other hand, in contrast to what we anticipated, the frequency of GMP was stable, and the percentage of CMP actually decreased significantly with age, defying our prediction that the frequency of components of the myeloid differentiation pathway, such as CMP, GMP, and megakaryocyte–erythrocyte progenitor (MEP), may increase in aged mice, if myeloid-biased HSC clones increase with age (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow analysis data in Figure 1B showing GMP frequencies across age groups.

claim: The percentage of CMP decreased significantly with age.
source: On the other hand, in contrast to what we anticipated, the frequency of GMP was stable, and the percentage of CMP actually decreased significantly with age, defying our prediction that the frequency of components of the myeloid differentiation pathway, such as CMP, GMP, and megakaryocyte–erythrocyte progenitor (MEP), may increase in aged mice, if myeloid-biased HSC clones increase with age (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow analysis data in Figure 1B showing CMP frequencies across age groups.

claim: Age-associated transition patterns of immunophenotypically defined HSC and CMP in bone marrow were not paralleled with myeloid cells in peripheral blood.
source: Our analysis of hematopoietic alternations with age revealed that age-associated transition patterns of immunophenotypically defined HSC and CMP in BM were not paralleled with myeloid cell in PB (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1C examining the ratio of aged to young frequencies across different cell types.

claim: Hoxb5 is exclusively expressed in bulk-HSCs in aged mice.
source: We observed that Hoxb5 was exclusively expressed in bulk-HSCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2A showing Hoxb5 reporter expression in different hematopoietic populations from 2-year-old mice.

claim: Only recipients receiving aged Hoxb5+ HSCs exhibited continuous hematopoiesis 16 weeks after primary transplantation.
source: We observed that only recipients receiving aged Hoxb5+ HSCs exhibited continuous hematopoiesis 16 weeks after primary transplantation (Figure 2C, E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by transplantation assay data shown in Figure 2C, E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A tracking donor chimerism over time.

claim: Only recipients receiving Hoxb5+ HSCs exhibited robust hematopoiesis throughout the period of observation in secondary transplantation.
source: In secondary transplantation analysis, only recipients receiving Hoxb5+ HSCs exhibited robust hematopoiesis throughout the period of observation, indicating that Hoxb5 can be used as a specific marker of LT-HSCs in aged mice, as well as young mice (Figure 2D, F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by secondary transplantation data shown in Figure 2D, F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hoxb5 can be used as a specific marker of LT-HSCs in aged mice, as well as young mice.
source: In secondary transplantation analysis, only recipients receiving Hoxb5+ HSCs exhibited robust hematopoiesis throughout the period of observation, indicating that Hoxb5 can be used as a specific marker of LT-HSCs in aged mice, as well as young mice (Figure 2D, F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from transplantation experiments showing that only Hoxb5+ cells maintain long-term reconstitution capacity in both young and aged mice.

claim: The kinetics of the proportion of myeloid cells in peripheral blood were similar across primary and secondary transplantation of aged LT-HSCs.
source: However, we found that the kinetics of the proportion of myeloid cells in PB were similar across the primary and the secondary transplantation (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2G showing myeloid output kinetics across primary and secondary transplantation.

claim: The myeloid lineage proportions from young and aged LT-HSCs were nearly comparable during the observation period after co-transplantation.
source: Then, we found that the myeloid lineage proportions from young and aged LT-HSCs were nearly comparable during the observation period after transplantation (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Supported by co-transplantation assay data shown in Figure 3B, C comparing lineage output from young versus aged LT-HSCs in the same recipients.

claim: The reconstitution ratio between young and aged LT-HSCs was almost the same across all lineages.
source: We confirmed again that the reconstitution ratio was almost the same across all lineages, although bulk hematopoiesis derived from young LT-HSCs predominated (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by competitive analysis data in Figure 3D showing the ratio of young to aged LT-HSC-derived cells across different cell types.

claim: The differentiation potential of LT-HSCs remains unchanged throughout their lives.
source: These results indicate that the differentiation potential of LT-HSCs remains unchanged throughout their lives.
evidence: Inferred from co-transplantation experiments showing comparable lineage output between young and aged LT-HSCs.

claim: Aged bulk-HSCs exhibited a myeloid-skewed phenotype compared to young bulk-HSCs.
source: As previously described, we observed that aged bulk-HSC exhibited a myeloid-skewed phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by co-transplantation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C comparing young and aged bulk-HSC lineage output.

claim: Aged bulk-HSC reconstitution exhibited higher reconstitution of myeloid cells compared to young bulk-HSCs.
source: Additionally, we observed that aged bulk-HSC reconstitution exhibited higher reconstitution of myeloid cells compared to young bulk-HSCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by competitive analysis data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing differential myeloid output between young and aged bulk-HSCs.

claim: Neither aged LT-HSCs nor aged ST-HSCs exhibited myeloid/lymphoid gene set enrichment.
source: Neither aged LT-HSCs nor aged ST-HSCs exhibited myeloid/lymphoid gene set enrichment, while shared myeloid-related genes tended to be enriched in aged bulk-HSCs, although this enrichment was not statistically significant (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) results shown in Figure 4F, G using defined myeloid and lymphoid signature genes.

claim: Shared myeloid-related genes tended to be enriched in aged bulk-HSCs, although this enrichment was not statistically significant.
source: Neither aged LT-HSCs nor aged ST-HSCs exhibited myeloid/lymphoid gene set enrichment, while shared myeloid-related genes tended to be enriched in aged bulk-HSCs, although this enrichment was not statistically significant (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: Supported by GSEA results in Figure 4F showing a trend toward myeloid gene enrichment in aged bulk-HSCs that did not reach statistical significance.

claim: Donor-derived hematopoiesis eventually becomes lymphocyte dominant in peripheral blood of ST-HSC recipients over time.
source: As we previously reported (Chen et al., 2016), donor-derived hematopoiesis eventually becomes lymphocyte dominant in PB of ST-HSC recipients over time (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by transplantation data in Figure 5B showing kinetics of lymphoid cell frequency in ST-HSC recipients, and cited from previous work (Chen et al., 2016).

claim: The vast majority of T cell subsets in ST-HSC recipients are memory cells.
source: Subsequently, it was determined that the vast majority of T cell subsets are memory cells (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: Supported by T cell phenotyping data shown in Figure 5C, D demonstrating predominance of memory T cells in ST-HSC recipients.

claim: Recipients receiving ST-HSCs lacked any bulk-HSCs in their bone marrow.
source: In addition, unlike recipients receiving LT-HSCs, recipients receiving ST-HSCs lacked any bulk-HSCs in their BM (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow analysis data in Figure 5E, F showing absence of donor bulk-HSCs in ST-HSC recipients.

claim: Lymphoid-biased hematopoiesis observed after transplantation of ST-HSCs is due to persistence of memory-type lymphocytes in peripheral blood, rather than to de novo lymphopoiesis from lymphoid-biased HSC clones.
source: These results strongly suggest that lymphoid-biased hematopoiesis observed after transplantation of ST-HSCs is due to persistence of memory-type lymphocytes in PB, rather than to de novo lymphopoiesis from lymphoid-biased HSC clones.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ST-HSC recipients have memory T cells but lack HSCs in bone marrow, suggesting no ongoing lymphopoiesis.

claim: The ratio of ST-HSC to LT-HSC decreased with age.
source: To verify this hypothesis, we examined the kinetics of the LT-HSC/ST-HSC ratio in the bulk-HSC population, revealing the ratio of ST-HSC to LT-HSC decreased with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing age-associated changes in the frequency of LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs within the bulk-HSC fraction.

claim: Recipient mice transplanted with a 5:5 LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio began to exhibit more myeloid-biased hematopoiesis 8 weeks after transplantation.
source: Four weeks after transplantation, PB analysis revealed that both groups had comparable patterns of hematopoiesis. In contrast, recipient mice transplanted with a 5:5 ratio began to exhibit more myeloid-biased hematopoiesis 8 weeks after transplantation, and by week 16, they produced significantly more myeloid cells than the other group (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by transplantation data in Figure 6B-D showing temporal changes in lineage output based on LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio.

claim: By week 16, recipient mice transplanted with a 5:5 LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio produced significantly more myeloid cells than those transplanted with a 2:8 ratio.
source: Four weeks after transplantation, PB analysis revealed that both groups had comparable patterns of hematopoiesis. In contrast, recipient mice transplanted with a 5:5 ratio began to exhibit more myeloid-biased hematopoiesis 8 weeks after transplantation, and by week 16, they produced significantly more myeloid cells than the other group (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6B-D showing significantly higher myeloid cell frequency at 16 weeks in the 5:5 ratio group.

claim: Lymphoid lineage output in recipient mice transplanted with aged HSCs at a 2:8 LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio was significantly greater than those with a 5:5 ratio.
source: PB analysis revealed that lymphoid lineage output in the recipient mice transplanted with a 2:8 ratio was significantly greater than those with a 5:5 ratio (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D showing increased lymphoid output with higher ST-HSC proportion.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis observed following transplantation of aged HSCs was caused by a relative decrease in ST-HSC in the bulk-HSC compartment in aged mice rather than the selective expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones.
source: Based on these findings, we concluded that myeloid-biased hematopoiesis observed following transplantation of aged HSCs was caused by a relative decrease in ST-HSC in the bulk-HSC compartment in aged mice rather than the selective expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that manipulating the LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio recapitulates age-associated myeloid bias.

claim: Aged recipient mice receiving young LT-HSCs produced significantly more myeloid cells than young recipient mice.
source: PB analysis revealed that aged recipient mice receiving young LT-HSCs produced significantly more myeloid cells than young recipient mice (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Supported by transplantation data in Figure 7C-E comparing lineage output in young versus aged recipients.

claim: Percentages of CMP and GMP were stable or significantly lower in aged recipient mice than in young recipient mice.
source: Percentages of CMP and GMP, downstream components of myeloid differentiation, were stable or significantly lower in aged recipient mice than in young recipient mice, just as they were in non-treated aged mice (Figures 1B and 7F).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow analysis data in Figure 7F comparing progenitor frequencies between young and aged recipients.

claim: The percentage of common lymphoid progenitor did not differ between young and aged recipients.
source: In addition, the percentage of common lymphoid progenitor (CLP), a downstream component of lymphoid differentiation, did not differ between young and aged recipients (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow analysis data in Figure 7F showing CLP frequencies in young versus aged recipients.

claim: Intramedullary age-associated changes may not have a significant impact on LT-HSC differentiation.
source: In contrast to previous studies (Pinho et al., 2018; Ergen et al., 2012), these findings suggested that intramedullary age-associated changes may not have a significant impact on LT-HSC differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from bone marrow analysis showing similar progenitor frequencies between young and aged recipients, contrasting with cited previous studies (Pinho et al., 2018; Ergen et al., 2012).

claim: Donor cells were not microscopically detectable in the majority of aged recipient mice in thymus and spleen.
source: Donor cells were not microscopically detectable in the majority of aged recipient mice (Figure 7G, I), and quantitative analysis using a flow cytometer revealed that the frequency of donor cells in spleens and thymi of aged recipients was significantly lower than in young recipients (Figure 7H, J).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and flow cytometry data in Figure 7G-J showing reduced donor cell presence in aged recipient lymphoid organs.

claim: The frequency of donor cells in spleens and thymi of aged recipients was significantly lower than in young recipients.
source: Donor cells were not microscopically detectable in the majority of aged recipient mice (Figure 7G, I), and quantitative analysis using a flow cytometer revealed that the frequency of donor cells in spleens and thymi of aged recipients was significantly lower than in young recipients (Figure 7H, J).
evidence: Supported by quantitative flow cytometry data in Figure 7H, J comparing donor cell frequencies in lymphoid organs.

claim: The process of lymphoid lineage differentiation is impaired in the spleens and thymi of aged mice compared to young mice.
source: These findings suggest that myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to a relative decrease in the ratio of mature lymphocytes in PB, resulting from inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the BM, such as in the thymus and spleen, rather than a significant change in cell differentiation caused by the intramedullary environment.
evidence: Inferred from observations that donor cells are reduced in aged thymi and spleens but progenitors are unchanged in bone marrow.

claim: Myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to a relative decrease in the ratio of mature lymphocytes in peripheral blood, resulting from inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the bone marrow.
source: These findings suggest that myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to a relative decrease in the ratio of mature lymphocytes in PB, resulting from inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the BM, such as in the thymus and spleen, rather than a significant change in cell differentiation caused by the intramedullary environment.
evidence: Inferred from combined observations of unchanged bone marrow progenitors but reduced lymphoid organ function in aged mice.

claim: Age-related changes in individuals are deeply correlated with progressive attenuation of cellular functions in tissue stem cells of organs.
source: Age-associated changes in individuals are deeply correlated with progressive attenuation of cellular functions in tissue stem cells of organs (Jones and Rando, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones and Rando, 2011.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells possess self-renewal capacity and multipotency.
source: In the hematopoietic system, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which possess self-renewal capacity and multipotency (Spangrude et al., 1988; Weissman and Shizuru, 2008; Majeti et al., 2007), are responsible for various hematopoietic alterations with age, such as reduced self-renewal capacity (Morrison et al., 1996) and myeloid-biased hematopoiesis (Muller-Sieburg et al., 2004; Challen et al., 2010) due to their functional decline.
evidence: Supported by citations to Spangrude et al., 1988; Weissman and Shizuru, 2008; Majeti et al., 2007.

claim: HSCs are responsible for various hematopoietic alterations with age, such as reduced self-renewal capacity and myeloid-biased hematopoiesis due to their functional decline.
source: In the hematopoietic system, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which possess self-renewal capacity and multipotency (Spangrude et al., 1988; Weissman and Shizuru, 2008; Majeti et al., 2007), are responsible for various hematopoietic alterations with age, such as reduced self-renewal capacity (Morrison et al., 1996) and myeloid-biased hematopoiesis (Muller-Sieburg et al., 2004; Challen et al., 2010) due to their functional decline.
evidence: Supported by citations to Morrison et al., 1996; Muller-Sieburg et al., 2004; Challen et al., 2010.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis potentially reduces response to infections.
source: For example, myeloid-biased hematopoiesis potentially reduces response to infections (Webster, 2000), reduces vaccination efficacy (Crooke et al., 2019), and increases myeloid malignancy (Rossi et al., 2008) in aged individuals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Webster, 2000.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis reduces vaccination efficacy.
source: For example, myeloid-biased hematopoiesis potentially reduces response to infections (Webster, 2000), reduces vaccination efficacy (Crooke et al., 2019), and increases myeloid malignancy (Rossi et al., 2008) in aged individuals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crooke et al., 2019.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis increases myeloid malignancy in aged individuals.
source: For example, myeloid-biased hematopoiesis potentially reduces response to infections (Webster, 2000), reduces vaccination efficacy (Crooke et al., 2019), and increases myeloid malignancy (Rossi et al., 2008) in aged individuals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2008.

claim: Transplantation of aged HSCs exhibits more myeloid-biased differentiation in young recipient mice than transplantation of young HSCs.
source: Based on the experimental observation that transplantation of aged HSCs exhibits more myeloid-biased differentiation in young recipient mice than transplantation of young HSCs, this phenotype has been thought to originate in cell-intrinsic changes in the HSC compartment (Geiger et al., 2013; de Haan and Lazare, 2018; Schultz and Sinclair, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2013; de Haan and Lazare, 2018; Schultz and Sinclair, 2016.

claim: Myeloid-biased phenotype after aged HSC transplantation leads to the suggestion that myeloid-biased HSC clones selectively expand with age.
source: A myeloid-biased phenotype after aged HSC transplantation leads to the suggestion that myeloid-biased HSC clones selectively expand with age (Cho et al., 2008; Pang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cho et al., 2008; Pang et al., 2011.

claim: Transcriptome and epigenetic analyses show that a set of genes related to myeloid differentiation is significantly enriched in aged HSCs compared to young HSCs.
source: Transcriptome and epigenetic analyses showing that a set of genes related to myeloid differentiation is significantly enriched in aged HSCs compared to young HSCs (Rossi et al., 2005; Grover et al., 2016) further supports this hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossi et al., 2005; Grover et al., 2016.

claim: Aged lymphoid-biased HSCs still demonstrate the same level of lymphopoiesis as their younger counterparts, despite exhibiting a myeloid-biased gene expression pattern.
source: On the other hand, some reports support a different point of view in light of experimental evidence showing that aged lymphoid-biased HSCs still demonstrate the same level of lymphopoiesis as their younger counterparts, despite exhibiting a myeloid-biased gene expression pattern (Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019.

claim: The increment of myeloid progenitors with age was not consistently demonstrated in earlier research.
source: However, the increment of such progenitors with age was not consistently demonstrated in earlier research (Rossi et al., 2005; Rundberg Nilsson et al., 2016; Min et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossi et al., 2005; Rundberg Nilsson et al., 2016; Min et al., 2006.

claim: A mathematical model demonstrated that aging had no effect on the daily production of CMP supplied from multipotent progenitors.
source: Additionally, a mathematical model demonstrated that aging had no effect on the daily production of CMP supplied from multipotent progenitors (MPPs) (Busch et al., 2015; Dorshkind et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Busch et al., 2015; Dorshkind et al., 2020.

claim: Selective expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones is the most widely accepted hypothesis to explain myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aging.
source: As such, while selective expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones is the most widely accepted hypothesis to explain myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aging (Mejia-Ramirez and Florian, 2020; SanMiguel et al., 2020), other mechanisms may exist in light of the inconsistent cellular behavior of progenitor fractions relative to HSCs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mejia-Ramirez and Florian, 2020; SanMiguel et al., 2020.

claim: Mouse HSC research on aging has used mice aged 18 months or older.
source: Mouse HSC research on aging has used mice aged 18 months or older (Challen et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2008; Rossi et al., 2005; Grover et al., 2016; Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Rundberg Nilsson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Challen et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2008; Rossi et al., 2005; Grover et al., 2016; Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Rundberg Nilsson et al., 2016.

claim: Hoxb5 exclusively marks LT-HSCs in young mice.
source: We previously reported that Hoxb5 exclusively marks LT-HSCs in young mice (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Immunophenotypically defined HSCs possess heterogeneity associated with self-renewal capacity, suggesting the existence of at least two different populations: long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs) and short-term hematopoietic stem cells (ST-HSCs).
source: Other studies have reported that immunophenotypically defined HSCs possess heterogeneity associated with self-renewal capacity, suggesting the existence of at least two different populations in the HSC compartment, long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs) and short-term hematopoietic stem cells (ST-HSCs) (Morrison and Weissman, 1994; Spangrude et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morrison and Weissman, 1994; Spangrude et al., 1995.

claim: LT-HSCs have extensive self-renewal capacity, while ST-HSCs lose their self-renewal capacity within a short period.
source: Since LT-HSCs have extensive self-renewal capacity, while ST-HSCs lose their self-renewal capacity within a short period, LT-HSCs are thought to persist in the BM throughout life and to enrich age-associated changes compared to ST-HSCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about HSC heterogeneity and self-renewal capacity differences.

claim: LT-HSCs are thought to persist in the bone marrow throughout life and to enrich age-associated changes compared to ST-HSCs.
source: Since LT-HSCs have extensive self-renewal capacity, while ST-HSCs lose their self-renewal capacity within a short period, LT-HSCs are thought to persist in the BM throughout life and to enrich age-associated changes compared to ST-HSCs.
evidence: Inferred from the differential self-renewal capacity between LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs.

claim: Transplanted ST-HSCs maintain lymphocyte production while rapidly losing myeloid lineage production in recipients.
source: First, we revisited our previous study (Chen et al., 2016), which demonstrated that transplanted ST-HSCs maintain lymphocyte production while rapidly losing myeloid lineage production in recipients.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Donor cells obtained from primary recipients receiving ST-HSCs do not undergo hematopoiesis in secondary transplantation.
source: Given that donor cells obtained from primary recipients receiving ST-HSCs do not undergo hematopoiesis in secondary transplantation (Chen et al., 2016), it is likely that all ST-HSCs have already lost their ability to self-renew and have disappeared from the HSC fraction in primary recipients.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: All ST-HSCs have already lost their ability to self-renew and have disappeared from the HSC fraction in primary recipients.
source: Given that donor cells obtained from primary recipients receiving ST-HSCs do not undergo hematopoiesis in secondary transplantation (Chen et al., 2016), it is likely that all ST-HSCs have already lost their ability to self-renew and have disappeared from the HSC fraction in primary recipients.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ST-HSC-derived cells fail to reconstitute in secondary transplantation.

claim: Almost 80% of differentially expressed genes in mouse HSC aging are poorly reproducible across datasets.
source: A recent comprehensive analysis of mouse HSC aging using multiple RNA-seq datasets claimed that almost 80% of differentially expressed genes are poorly reproducible across datasets (Flohr Svendsen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flohr Svendsen et al., 2021.

claim: Almost 80% of genes are not shared when comparing three representative myeloid/lymphoid gene sets.
source: In fact, we found that almost 80% of genes are not shared when we compare three representative myeloid/lymphoid gene sets (Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013; Chambers et al., 2007; Pronk et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 4D, E comparing gene sets from Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013; Chambers et al., 2007; Pronk et al., 2007.

claim: Most genes in myeloid/lymphoid gene sets were only used in a single gene set.
source: Additionally, most genes were only used in a single gene set (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4D, E.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis has been suggested as a potential reason for the decline in acquired immunity in the elderly.
source: Age-related, myeloid-biased hematopoiesis has been suggested as a potential reason for the decline in acquired immunity in the elderly (Geiger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geiger et al., 2013.

claim: Age-related changes in the ratio of ST-HSCs to LT-HSCs in bulk-HSCs are responsible for myeloid-biased hematopoiesis.
source: By isolating LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs, respectively, we discovered that age-related changes in the ratio of ST-HSCs to LT-HSCs in bulk-HSCs are responsible for myeloid-biased hematopoiesis.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that manipulating the LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio recapitulates age-associated myeloid bias.

claim: When aged bulk-HSCs were transplanted into young mice, post-transplant hematopoiesis in recipient mice was significantly biased toward myeloid in peripheral blood compared to transplantation of young bulk-HSCs.
source: When aged bulk-HSCs were transplanted into young mice, post-transplant hematopoiesis in recipient mice was significantly biased toward myeloid in PB compared to transplantation of young bulk-HSCs (Beerman et al., 2010; Dykstra et al., 2011; Sudo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beerman et al., 2010; Dykstra et al., 2011; Sudo et al., 2000.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis derived from aged bulk-HSCs has been considered as evidence supporting expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones with aging.
source: Historically, this myeloid-biased hematopoiesis derived from aged bulk-HSCs has been considered as evidence supporting expansion of myeloid-biased HSC clones with aging (Geiger et al., 2013; Haan and Lazare, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2013; Haan and Lazare, 2018.

claim: Blockage of lymphoid hematopoiesis in aged mice results in myeloid-skewed hematopoiesis through alternative mechanisms.
source: Other studies suggest that blockage of lymphoid hematopoiesis in aged mice results in myeloid-skewed hematopoiesis through alternative mechanisms. However, this result should be interpreted carefully, since Busulfan was used for myeloablative treatment in this study (Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019, with caveat about experimental design.

claim: Age-related myeloid-biased hematopoiesis cannot be attributed to an increase in myeloid-biased HSCs, at least among LT-HSCs.
source: Therefore, we inferred that age-related myeloid-biased hematopoiesis cannot be attributed to an increase in myeloid-biased HSCs, at least among LT-HSCs.
evidence: Inferred from observations that aged LT-HSCs show comparable differentiation to young LT-HSCs and lack myeloid gene enrichment.

claim: It has been reported that myeloid-biased HSCs have a more persistent capacity for self-renewal.
source: On the other hand, it has been reported that myeloid-biased HSCs have a more persistent capacity for self-renewal (Muller-Sieburg et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller-Sieburg et al., 2004.

claim: Myeloid cell production in peripheral blood was greater when LT-HSCs were transplanted, while ST-HSC transplantation resulted in a considerable increase in lymphoid cell production.
source: In fact, in our prior investigation comparing PB 16 weeks post-transplant, myeloid cell production in PB was greater when LT-HSCs were transplanted, while ST-HSC transplantation resulted in a considerable increase in lymphoid cell production (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The myeloid-producing capacity of LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs 4 weeks post-transplantation is equivalent.
source: However, the myeloid-producing capacity of LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs 4 weeks post-transplantation is equivalent (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: 16 weeks after transplantation, ST-HSC transplant recipients demonstrate negligible myeloid development and a predominance of lymphocytes, unlike LT-HSC transplant recipients.
source: In contrast, 16 weeks after transplantation, ST-HSC transplant recipients demonstrate negligible myeloid development and a predominance of lymphocytes, unlike LT-HSC transplant recipients (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: When ST-HSC-transplanted bone marrow cells are employed as donors for secondary transplantation, no donor-cell-derived hematopoiesis is detected in recipients.
source: When ST-HSC-transplanted BM cells are employed as donors for secondary transplantation, no donor-cell-derived hematopoiesis is detected in recipients (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: ST-HSCs lose their capacity for self-renewal earlier after transplantation than LT-HSCs.
source: These results indicate that ST-HSCs lose their capacity for self-renewal earlier after transplantation than LT-HSCs.
evidence: Inferred from observations that ST-HSCs fail to reconstitute in secondary transplantation and are absent from bone marrow.

claim: ST-HSCs may have been erroneously classified as lymphoid-biased HSCs due to the preservation of memory lymphocytes with a long half-life in the peripheral circulation, despite the absence of de novo hematopoiesis following transplantation of ST-HSCs.
source: In other words, ST-HSCs may have been erroneously classified as lymphoid-biased HSCs due to the preservation of memory lymphocytes with a long half-life in the peripheral circulation, despite the absence of de novo hematopoiesis following transplantation of ST-HSCs.
evidence: Inferred from observations that ST-HSC recipients have memory T cells but no ongoing hematopoiesis.

claim: The bias toward myeloid and lymphoid lineages in post-transplant peripheral blood is not regulated by heterogeneity of multipotency, but by heterogeneity of self-renewal capacity.
source: These findings suggest that the bias toward myeloid and lymphoid lineages in post-transplant PB is not regulated by heterogeneity of multipotency, but by heterogeneity of self-renewal capacity.
evidence: Inferred from observations that LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs differ in self-renewal but not in initial differentiation capacity.

claim: Cell interaction with niche cells in bone marrow is altered with age.
source: Some findings suggest that cell interaction with niche cells in BM is altered (Pinho et al., 2018), whereas others claim that chronic inflammation in aged mice lowers production of lymphoid progenitors and induces myeloid-biased hematopoiesis (Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Ergen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pinho et al., 2018.

claim: Chronic inflammation in aged mice lowers production of lymphoid progenitors and induces myeloid-biased hematopoiesis.
source: Some findings suggest that cell interaction with niche cells in BM is altered (Pinho et al., 2018), whereas others claim that chronic inflammation in aged mice lowers production of lymphoid progenitors and induces myeloid-biased hematopoiesis (Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Ergen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Montecino-Rodriguez et al., 2019; Ergen et al., 2012.

claim: Myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the bone marrow, such as in the thymus and spleen, rather than a significant change in cell differentiation caused by the intramedullary environment.
source: These findings suggest that myeloid cells increase in aging mice due to a relative decrease in the ratio of mature lymphocytes in PB, resulting from inhibition of lymphocyte maturation outside the BM, such as in the thymus and spleen, rather than a significant change in cell differentiation caused by the intramedullary environment.
evidence: Inferred from observations that bone marrow progenitors are unchanged but lymphoid organs show reduced donor cell presence in aged recipients.

claim: Attempts have been made to restore thymus function in aged mice by administering keratinocyte growth factor.
source: Attempts have been made in the past to restore thymus function in aged mice by administering keratinocyte growth factor (Rossi et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2007b.

claim: In aged mice, lymphocyte hematopoiesis recovers with keratinocyte growth factor treatment.
source: Indeed, in aged mice, lymphocyte hematopoiesis recovers, which is consistent with our results that the extramedullary environment influences the myeloid-bias phenotype in PB (Rossi et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2007b.

claim: Recovery of the lymphocyte fraction in peripheral blood is delayed in elderly donors, compared to young donors.
source: It has been clinically documented that recovery of the lymphocyte fraction in PB is delayed in elderly donors, compared to young donors (González-Vicent et al., 2017; Baron et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to González-Vicent et al., 2017; Baron et al., 2006.

claim: Lymphocyte recovery is delayed in elderly patients compared to younger patients.
source: It has also been noted that lymphocyte recovery is delayed in elderly patients compared to younger patients (Berger et al., 2008; van der Maas et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berger et al., 2008; van der Maas et al., 2021.

claim: Age-related loss in thymus and spleen functions has been recorded in humans.
source: Age-related loss in thymus and spleen functions has been recorded in humans, implying that the same mechanism is acting as in our mouse observations.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about age-related decline in human lymphoid organ function.

claim: Cellular differentiation in the peripheral blood after transplantation can vary by changing transplantation conditions, ultimately altering self-renewal ability.
source: In addition to this report, we have also shown that cellular differentiation in the PB after transplantation can vary by changing transplantation conditions, ultimately altering self-renewal ability (Sakamaki et al., 2021; Nishi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sakamaki et al., 2021; Nishi et al., 2022.

claim: The ratio of LT-HSC/ST-HSCs is important in age-related myeloid-skewed hematopoiesis as an HSC-dependent factor.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated for the first time that the ratio of LT-HSC/ST-HSC is important in age-related myeloid-skewed hematopoiesis as an HSC-dependent factor and that aging-related thymus and spleen dysfunction also contributes significantly as an HSC-independent factor.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that manipulating the LT-HSC:ST-HSC ratio recapitulates age-associated myeloid bias.

claim: Aging-related thymus and spleen dysfunction contributes significantly to myeloid-biased hematopoiesis as an HSC-independent factor.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated for the first time that the ratio of LT-HSC/ST-HSC is important in age-related myeloid-skewed hematopoiesis as an HSC-dependent factor and that aging-related thymus and spleen dysfunction also contributes significantly as an HSC-independent factor.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing reduced lymphoid output in aged recipients despite normal bone marrow progenitors.

claim: Myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice originates due to alteration of the ratio between LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs rather than in heterogeneous HSC clones with various cell fates.
source: Thus, we demonstrate that myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in aged mice originates due to alteration of the ratio between LT-HSCs and ST-HSCs rather than in heterogeneous HSC clones with various cell fates.
evidence: Inferred from combined observations that LT-HSCs maintain constant differentiation potential but their ratio to ST-HSCs changes with age.

claim: Young and aged LT-HSCs co-transplanted into the same recipients demonstrated nearly equivalent myeloid lineage output.
source: Utilizing the Hoxb5 reporter system to prospectively isolate long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs) and short-term HSCs (ST-HSCs), we found that young and aged LT-HSCs co-transplanted into the same recipients demonstrated nearly equivalent myeloid lineage output, contrary to the theory of myeloid-biased HSC clones.
evidence: Supported by co-transplantation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transcriptomics indicated no significant myeloid gene enrichment in aged LT-HSCs compared to their young counterparts.
source: Transcriptomics indicated no significant myeloid gene enrichment in aged LT-HSCs compared to their young counterparts.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis and GSEA results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transplanting reconstituted young HSCs with the ratio of LT/ST-HSCs seen in aged mice can significantly skew the lineage output to myeloid cells.
source: Instead, transplanting reconstituted young HSCs with the ratio of LT/ST-HSCs seen in aged mice can significantly skew the lineage output to myeloid cells.
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6 comparing 2:8 versus 5:5 LT:ST ratios.

claim: The niche environment in the bone marrow minimally affects myeloid-biased hematopoiesis.
source: In addition, while the niche environment in the bone marrow minimally affects myeloid-biased hematopoiesis, aged thymi and spleens substantially hinder lymphoid hematopoiesis, resulting in further myeloid domination.
evidence: Inferred from observations that bone marrow progenitor frequencies are similar between young and aged recipients.

claim: Aged thymi and spleens substantially hinder lymphoid hematopoiesis, resulting in further myeloid domination.
source: In addition, while the niche environment in the bone marrow minimally affects myeloid-biased hematopoiesis, aged thymi and spleens substantially hinder lymphoid hematopoiesis, resulting in further myeloid domination.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7 showing reduced donor cells in aged thymi and spleens.
